tldr: This paper presents a novel retargeting method and a high-quality dataset for transferring cooperative carrying motions—where two humans coordinate to transport large boxes—to two humanoid robots without breakdown. By jointly optimizing object-mediated grasp relationships and whole-body ground support, the method produces stable cooperative carrying motions free of penetration and foot sliding.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of the proposed method. Starting from nominal synchronized motions from the CoCarry dataset, the framework jointly refines both robots around a prescribed object trajectory using cooperation-aware object-local hand anchors and two complementary relational mesh structures: upper-body object interaction and lower-body ground support.
overview:
Whole-body control for single humanoid robots has progressed rapidly in recent years. However, the difficulty spikes when two robots must work together to carry a single heavy object. This cooperative carrying task requires far more than plausible individual motions. The positions and orientations of all four hands on the object, the relative configuration between the two robots, and whole-body ground support must remain completely consistent throughout the task. Otherwise, the object will be dropped or the robots will collide with each other.

Applying existing motion retargeting methods (techniques that convert human movements into robot joint trajectories) separately to each person leads to issues. Even if each robot's individual pose looks natural, their hands often penetrate deep into the object or lose contact entirely. To solve this, the authors constructed "CoCarry," a large-scale two-person cooperative carrying dataset, and developed "Contact–Support-Structured Retargeting," which jointly optimizes both robots within a single optimization loop.

The method defines compatible contact points (anchors) for all four hands on the object surface, and enforces geometric relations by decoupling the upper body as an "object-relative interaction structure" and the lower body as a "ground-relative support structure." The authors validated their approach on physical A3 humanoids, Unitree G1 robots, and the external CORE4D dataset, followed by physics simulation and real-world experiments. The results demonstrate that the generated trajectories serve directly as effective references for physical control.
contributions: Construction of the CoCarry dataset, featuring 220 two-person cooperative carrying sequences (approximately 61 minutes) spanning 21 task schemes, 5 object geometries, and 4 terrain types.
Proposal of a joint retargeting method using cooperation-aware hand anchors to maintain four-hand contact consistency, alongside complementary decoupled upper- and lower-body relational meshes.

Demonstration of highly accurate trajectory generation on A3 and Unitree G1 robots, reducing object penetration duration by roughly 70% compared to baseline methods and achieving over 99% contact preservation.
Hardware demonstration of dual-humanoid cooperative carrying on two physical A3 humanoids using reinforcement learning imitation driven by the generated reference trajectories.

sections.heading: Why is retargeting two-person cooperative carrying so hard?
sections.summary: While individual humanoid control has advanced, two-robot cooperative carrying remains extremely difficult because geometric consistency across agents and between agents and the object is essential. This paper proposes the high-quality CoCarry dataset and a new retargeting method that jointly optimizes both robots.
sections.details:
Recent advances in imitation learning and motion retargeting using large-scale human motion data have dramatically improved the whole-body performance of individual humanoids. However, extending these technologies to dual-humanoid cooperative carrying immediately runs into major challenges. Cooperative carrying demands more than just natural individual motions. A shared grasp across both robots' hands, relative spatial configurations, and whole-body support balance against the ground must remain strictly consistent across the entire task.

Existing human-to-robot motion retargeting techniques (such as GMR and OmniRetarget) are designed for single robots or simple interactions, retargeting each human motion independently to each robot. This is the primary pitfall. No matter how natural the individual motions appear in isolation, placing the two robots side by side easily breaks the coordination: hands fail to reach the object, fingertips penetrate deep inside it, or the robots push against one another and slip on the floor. In short, successful individual retargeting does not guarantee successful cooperative retargeting.

To tackle this, the authors collected "CoCarry," a fully synchronized two-person motion dataset, and developed "Contact–Support-Structured Retargeting," which jointly optimizes both robots around the same object trajectory. Starting from nominal individual motions, the method introduces cooperative four-hand grasp anchors and decoupled structural constraints for the upper and lower body, successfully producing consistent, coordinated reference trajectories.

sections.heading: Limitations of prior work and unique positioning in cooperative carrying
sections.summary: While human interaction datasets and single-robot retargeting methods exist, datasets specialized for continuous, dynamic cooperative carrying were lacking. This work focuses on upstream dataset construction and trajectory generation, bridging the gap to downstream physical control.
sections.details:
### II-A Human Interaction and Cooperative Motion Datasets
Datasets capturing human interactions and object manipulations—such as Inter-X, CORE4D, and GRAB—have grown in recent years. However, very few focus on continuous, dynamic cooperative carrying, where two people lift, transport, navigate steps, and place heavy objects. CoCarry fills this gap by recording fully synchronized two-person motions, rigid-body object trajectories, and time-varying hand-object contact priors along a single, unified timeline.

### II-B Humanoid Motion Retargeting
Techniques that map human kinematics to robot structures include GMR, which relies on geometric mappings, and OmniRetarget, which preserves object relationships. However, applying these independently to two robots provides no guarantee of relative consistency between them. The proposed method takes a novel approach by using single-robot retargeting (GMR) as an initialization, and then performing joint optimization that couples both robots together.

### II-C Humanoid Imitation Learning and Cooperative Control
Reinforcement learning-based physics simulation imitation methods like DeepMimic and AMP have achieved major success on single humanoids. Rather than replacing physical controllers, the proposed method plays a complementary role upstream: it generates physically and geometrically sound cooperative reference trajectories for downstream controllers to track.

sections.heading: The CoCarry dataset: 220 synchronized cooperative carrying sequences
sections.summary: CoCarry is a large-scale dataset containing 220 sequences (roughly 61 minutes) with two participants and a shared object fully synchronized. It covers diverse tasks and object shapes, ranging from picking up and carrying to handovers and navigating stairs and ramps.
sections.details:
### III-A Dataset Scale and Task Coverage
CoCarry contains 220 sequences (approximately 61.1 minutes, 440,000 frames) recorded using a 120 Hz optical motion capture system. The tasks are divided into five families spanning 21 schemes:
- Pick-up / Place (6 schemes, 60 sequences): Lifting from and placing onto platforms of various heights
- Path / Turning (5 schemes, 60 sequences): Straight walking, S-curves, and 90-degree and 180-degree coordinated turns
- Terrain Navigation (4 schemes, 40 sequences): Ascending and descending ramps, as well as front-facing and sideways stair navigation
- Interaction Transitions (4 schemes, 40 sequences): Joining mid-motion, leaving, object handovers, and temporary set-downs
- Height Transitions (2 schemes, 20 sequences): Raising and lowering the object during transit
Additionally, five cuboid objects of varying sizes and aspect ratios are used, enforcing challenging conditions that alter arm reach and inter-robot carrying distance.

### III-B Synchronized Human–Object Representation
A critical feature of the dataset is that the two humans and the shared object are recorded in complete synchronization within the same timeline and world coordinate frame. To facilitate easy use as standard input for retargeting, each stream is resampled to 50 Hz while preserving frame-level correspondence.

### III-C Cooperative Interaction Priors
Beyond joint positions, the dataset provides contact point anchors $a_h$, normal vectors $\nu_h$, and time-varying contact activations for each of the four hands on the object surface. This allows the framework to represent dynamic tasks—such as releasing hands or shifting grasps mid-motion—in a unified manner, without assuming an unbroken hold.

captions.F2: Breakdown of the 220 sequences in the CoCarry dataset. Pick-up / Place and Path / Turning tasks each account for 27.3% (60 sequences each), accompanied by a well-balanced distribution of terrain navigation, transition, and height-change tasks.

sections.heading: Joint optimization via contact anchors and decoupled relational meshes
sections.summary: Starting from nominal GMR poses, both robots are jointly optimized at every frame using cooperative hand anchors on the object surface alongside upper-body (interaction) and lower-body (support) relational mesh constraints.
sections.details:
### IV-A Problem Formulation and GMR Initialization
Given two human motions and an object trajectory at time $t$, the goal is to solve for the combined robot joint configuration $q_t = (q_{1t}, q_{2t})$. First, individual GMR is applied separately to each robot to create an initial trajectory $\bar{q}_t$. While this initialization preserves natural human poses, it suffers from contact drift and object penetration. Using the prescribed object trajectory as a fixed reference frame, the method performs joint refinement (sequential optimization).

### IV-B Cooperative Hand Anchor Design and Activation
To ensure all four hands maintain coordinated grasp positions, anchors are defined in the object's local frame. Anchor selection relies on a composite score combining human hand proximity ($S_{\mathrm{prior}}$), grasp stability without slipping ($S_{\mathrm{stability}}$), and symmetrical, balanced four-hand placement ($S_{\mathrm{coop}}$).
Furthermore, to enforce constraints only when hands touch the object, a time-varying weight $\alpha_{ht} \in [0, 1]$ is smoothly computed from demonstrated and GMR hand-to-object distances, penalizing discrepancies between the palm orientation and the object surface normal.

### IV-C Decoupled Contact and Support Relational Meshes
Constraining the whole body within a single structure degrades foot stability. Therefore, the method builds two complementary geometric meshes:
- Upper-Body Interaction Mesh (Upper Mesh): Composed of shoulders, elbows, and hands of both robots along with sampled points on the object surface. Evaluated in the object-local frame, it preserves arm configurations and relative distances invariant to object motion.
- Lower-Body Support Mesh (Lower Mesh): Composed of pelvises, legs, and feet of both robots along with ground reference nodes. Evaluated in the world frame, it maintains stable stance and foot-ground support during walking and stair traversal.
Geometric preservation errors $E_U$ and $E_L$ are defined for each mesh using graph Laplacians.

### IV-D Dual-Humanoid Joint Cooperative Optimization
At each frame, a locally linearized quadratic program is solved. It minimizes mesh preservation errors, hand contact costs, foot contact costs, and deviations from the GMR initial poses, subject to joint limits, step-length bounds, and inter-robot collision avoidance constraints. Using the previous frame's solution as a warm start ensures smooth, physically plausible reference motions generated continuously for both robots.

sections.heading: Experimental results: 70% reduction in penetration and real-world dual-robot transport
sections.summary: The authors validated their method across all 220 sequences using two A3 humanoids, on the CORE4D dataset using Unitree G1 robots, and through physics simulation and real-world carrying trials. The results demonstrate contact accuracy and practical utility for control that far exceed baseline methods.
sections.details:
### V-A Experimental Setup and Metrics
Evaluations were conducted on two AgiBot A3 humanoids with motions generated at 50 Hz. Comparisons were made against individual GMR and OmniRetarget (both applied independently to each robot). Evaluation metrics included the fraction of frames with maintained intended contact (Contact Preservation), the fraction of frames where hands penetrated the object (Penetration Duration), maximum penetration depth, and unnecessary foot slip (Sliding Duration).

### V-B Comparative Results on the CoCarry Dataset
The proposed method achieved a 100% retargeting success rate across all 220 sequences. Contact preservation reached an almost perfect 0.9995. Penetration duration plummeted to 0.1925, representing relative reductions of 67.0% and 71.0% compared to GMR (0.5840) and OmniRetarget (0.6640), respectively. Maximum penetration depth was also the lowest at 0.0451 m. Although GMR showed lower foot sliding, hands penetrated deep into the object or lost contact entirely, rendering the motion unusable as a cooperative reference.

### V-C Ablation Studies
- Removing hand anchors: Even when contact proximity scores appeared high, penetration duration degraded sharply from 0.1925 to 0.6638. Proximity alone allows hands to intersect the object from incorrect orientations, highlighting the need for explicit cooperative anchors.
- Merging upper and lower meshes into a single whole-body mesh: Foot sliding duration worsened by approximately 88%, increasing from 0.1913 to 0.3600. Decoupling the interaction structure (object-local) from the support structure (ground-relative) directly ensures ground footing stability.

### V-D Generalization on CORE4D and Unitree G1
Testing on 200 sequences from the external CORE4D dataset using two Unitree G1 robots yielded 0.9906 contact preservation and zero measured foot sliding. This demonstrates high generalizability across differing robot embodiments and unseen objects (buckets, desks, chairs, etc.).

### V-E Physical Validation in Simulation and Real A3 Robots
Imitation policies were trained using reinforcement learning on top of the generated reference trajectories. In physics simulation, two A3 robots successfully approached, lifted, carried, and placed an unconstrained, physics-driven box. Furthermore, the controllers were deployed to two physical A3 humanoids, confirming stable cooperative carrying in the real world without human assistance.

captions.F6: Downstream task execution on two physical A3 humanoids and in physics simulation. Across the Lift, Carry, and Place phases, stable cooperative motions are realized based on the retargeted reference trajectories.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future outlook
sections.summary: This work introduces the CoCarry dataset and a contact-support-structured joint retargeting method. Successful carrying in both simulation and real-world hardware establishes a new foundation for multi-humanoid collaborative tasks.
sections.details:
This paper presents a new framework for accurately retargeting coordinated two-person carrying motions to dual humanoid robots. By pairing the high-quality CoCarry dataset with joint optimization using cooperative hand anchors and decoupled geometric meshes, the approach resolves the penetration and contact loss problems inherent in prior independent retargeting pipelines.

Validating the pipeline end-to-end—not only in simulation, but on physical humanoids—represents a major milestone toward practical deployment. In future work, the authors plan to expand to broader cooperative manipulation tasks beyond carrying, support heterogeneous multi-robot setups, and conduct extensive real-world benchmarks.

takeaways: "The sum of individual optima is not cooperative optimum": In multi-agent collaborative retargeting, using nominal individual poses as an initialization and performing joint optimization over a shared object is essential.

Decoupled coordinate frames are key: Structuring the upper body in an "object-local frame" and the lower body in a "ground-relative world frame" prevents foot sliding and hand penetration at the same time.

The pitfall of proximity metrics: Evaluating only the Euclidean distance between hands and the object can yield high scores even when hands penetrate deeply inside. Explicit anchors considering normal vectors and grasp balance are necessary.
limitations: The retargeting phase assumes a known (prescribed) object trajectory and does not perform online dynamic trajectory generation when disturbances alter object motion on the fly.

The method does not model contact dynamics like grasp or frictional forces directly, generating kinematic references from geometric constraints. Handling extremely heavy objects may require dynamic force adjustments.
While real-world validation was demonstrated on representative tasks using A3 humanoids, comprehensive hardware benchmarking across all 220 dataset tasks was not conducted.
